name: Significant Figures
description: Learn about Significant Figures and its applications in physics.

content.overview: Quick question: is 100 grams the same as 100.0 grams? They look almost identical, but they're actually telling you very different things about how carefully something was measured. That's what significant figures are all about—they tell you how much you can trust a number. {{viz:diagram-01}}
keyPoints: Significant figures = the digits in a number that carry real meaning about precision {{viz:diagram-02}}
Non-zero digits always count; leading zeros never do; trailing zeros only count with a decimal point
100 has 1 sig fig (ambiguous), but 100.0 has 4—the decimal point makes a big difference
Your final answer can only be as precise as your least precise measurement
content.whyItMatters: Sig figs keep you honest. Without them, you might report a measurement as more precise than it really is—like claiming you know something down to the millimeter when your ruler only measures centimeters. Scientists (and engineers building bridges!) rely on sig figs to communicate exactly how much they can trust a number.
